query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability to form and maintain a protective oxide layer above 900 °C is primarily determined by the alloy’s phase homogeneity. A single-phase solid solution ensures uniform diffusion and surface segregation of the reactive element (X = Si or Al) that can form stable, strain-accommodated oxides (e.g., SiO2 or Al2O3), while the presence of multiple phases leads to heterogeneous local compositions that promote uneven oxide growth and increased stresses, resulting in cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy prepared either as a single-phase homogeneous solid solution or as a multiphase heterogeneous solid solution, with X being Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled high-temperature oxidation experiments above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere on alloys differing in both X content (Si, Mn, or Al) and phase homogeneity (single-phase versus multiphase).
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures exceeding 900 °C in a controlled oxidative (or corrosive) environment, ensuring consistent thermal cycling and mechanical load conditions across samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural homogeneity, which governs the uniformity of elemental (especially X element) surface segregation and diffusion pathways that lead to continuous oxide scale formation.
generation.mechanism: In single-phase alloys, a uniform cationic environment allows the chosen reactive element (Si or Al) to segregate evenly to the surface and form a coherent, protective oxide layer that accommodates thermal strain. In contrast, multiphase alloys exhibit compositional inhomogeneities and phase boundaries that disrupt uniform oxide formation, favoring the development of localized stress fields that cause oxide cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys in a single-phase state containing Si or Al will exhibit continuous, adherent, and stable oxide layers during high-temperature exposures, whereas multiphase alloys—and those with Mn, which is less likely to form protective oxides—will display unstable oxide scales with increased cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: The baseline consists of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Mn and/or alloys deliberately processed to yield a multiphase structure, which are expected to form less coherent and more defect-prone oxide layers under identical exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys when exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. The behavior may not extrapolate to lower temperatures or different alloy systems without similar reactive elements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative differences in oxide layer thickness, stress accommodation, and spallation rates could be sensitive to slight variations in alloy composition, processing conditions, and environmental parameters. The interplay of additional minor alloying elements and thermal gradients remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with X = Si, Mn, and Al in both controlled single-phase and deliberately multiphase states. Expose these samples to an oxidative atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for a fixed duration. Characterize the surface oxide layers and evaluate their continuity and integrity.
measurements: Surface morphology and continuity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Phase composition and oxide structure via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Elemental distribution at the surface using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
Assessment of oxide layer cracking or spallation via optical microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the single-phase alloys containing Si or Al do not form significantly more coherent, continuous, and stable oxide layers compared to the multiphase and Mn-containing alloys under identical exposure conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Spinel-Type (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4 High-Entropy Oxide: Facile Preparation and Supercapacitor Performance

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have attracted more and more attention because of their unique structures and potential applications. In this work, (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4 HEO powders were synthesized via a facile solid-state reaction route. The confirmation of phase composition, the observation of microstructure, and the analysis of crystal structure, distribution of elements, and valences of elements were conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), respectively. Furthermore, a (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4/nickel foam ((FeCoCrMnZn)3O4/NF) electrode was prepared via a coating method, followed by the investigation of its supercapacitor performance. The results show that, after calcining (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4 powders at 900 °C for 2 h, a single spinel structure (FCC, Fd-3m, a = 0.8399 nm) was obtained with uniform distribution of Fe, Co, Cr, Mn, and Zn elements, the typical characteristic of a high-entropy oxide. Microstructure Evolution of FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 High Entropy Alloy during Powder Preparation, Laser Powder Bed Fusion, and Microplasma Spraying

Abstract: AbstractIn the present study, powder of FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA was manufactured by gas atomization process, and then used for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and microplasma spraying (MPS) technologies. The processes of phase composition and microstructure transformation during above mentioned processes and subsequent heat treatment were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) methods. It was found that gas atomization leads to a formation of dendrites of body centered cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich segregations on the peripheries of the dendrites. Annealing leads to an increase of element segregations till to decomposition of the BCC solid solution and formation of σ-phase and B2 phase.
